Rising Focus on Organic and Antibiotic-Free Poultry: Consumer demand for organic, free-range, and antibiotic-residue-free poultry products is growing. Farmers and entrepreneurs can tap into premium niche markets by adopting organic certifications and better rearing practices. 7 p. Demand for animal protein source: In addition to meeting the requirements of human beings there is a rise in demand for animal protein source from companion animal food sector and nutraceuticals. q. Scope for Environmental controlled Poultry Sheds: To modernize and transform the poultry sector in Andhra Pradesh through promotion of Environmentally Controlled (EC) Poultry Sheds, supported by scientific poultry farming practices, improved bio-security, climate- resilient infrastructure, efficient resource utilization, environmental sustainability, disease surveillance, waste management. 5.0. Scope for Rural Poultry Farming: The expansion of commercial poultry farming in urban areas has created a wide gap in the availability of eggs and chicken meat between urbanites and malnourished rural / tribal people. a) Nutrition and Food Security:  Protein deficiency is a common phenomenon in the diets of rural people as their diets are predominantly based on cereals alone which contain high energy and low protein nutrients.  By adopting the rural poultry farming, the high incidence of protein hunger in the rural population particularly in pregnant & lactating mothers and growing kids can be obviated. b) Low Investment, High Returns:  Backyard poultry farming will generate petty cash for house hold requirement in addition to providing a balanced food with in rural areas.

items.text: Feeding of the backyard poultry is also easy by using household wastes, farm products and green vegetation, besides free scavenging for waste grains and insects.  Backyard farming utilizes minimum inputs, least human attention and causes less environmental pollution. c) Employment Generation  Growing urban demand for free-range and organic poultry opens high- value markets for rural producers.  The eggs and meat of birds reared in the backyard farming fetches premium rates due to high consumer accept ability even in the urban 8 areas even though plenty of eggs and poultry meat from commercial units are available. Less fat content in meat of these birds makes it acceptable to even aged people. d) High Adaptability of Rural Poultry  These birds can thrive well under adverse environmental conditions like poor housing, poor management and poor feeding. These birds are sturdy and resistant to most of the common poultry diseases because of its high immune competence.  These birds can perform well with diets high in crude fiber and have better feed efficiency even with diets containing low energy and protein diets with common feed ingredients available in rural / tribal areas like rice bran, broken rice, small millets like finger millet, pearl millet etc. 6.0. Vision To continue Andhra Pradesh as the highest egg and poultry meat producing state in the Country with sustainable growth in Poultry Sector for economic prosperity and nutritional security. 7.0 Mission a. To create more domestic demand for eggs by exporting to other countries. b. To increase domestic consumption of eggs by promoting egg consumption in Anganwadies, midday meal programme in schools etc. c. To reduce cost of production of eggs and chicken. d. To ensure availability of skilled man power like farm managers, farm supervisors and vaccinators etc. e.

Policy Validity The provisions made in the Industrial Development Policy, MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy and Food processing Policy relevant to the Poultry Sector is valid upto the 25.10.2029 only. Therefore in alignment of above two policies the poultry policy is also proposed for validity upto 25.10.2029. 9.0. Current Scenario in Poultry Sector 9.1.0 Layers The poultry sector is geared for high growth. The domestic poultry industry in India, currently Rs.19827 Cr. in size, is growing at over 10 percent a year and is likely to reach Rs.50000 Cr. in real terms over the next 10 years.

items.text: The domestic poultry industry in India, currently Rs.19827 Cr. in size, is growing at over 10 percent a year and is likely to reach Rs.50000 Cr. in real terms over the next 10 years. Export markets are also likely to open up due to the fact that the subsidies on agricultural products are phased out internationally under WTO agreements and the new markets like Russia and Eastern Europe open up. Developed well; by making the quality and cost of eggs and poultry meat competitive, India’s poultry sector could also capture a significant share of the exports market currently dominated by large exporters such as the US and Thailand. India has emerged as the only country in the developing world with a self-reliant, technology-driven industry with the capability to produce every essential input for successful poultry farming, including indigenous genetic resource & breeding, world class poultry vaccines & medicines, specific-pathogen-free eggs (SPF), farms & hatchery automation systems, pelleted feed, egg processing, poultry processing, nationwide network of disease diagnostic laboratories & facilities for entrepreneurial development and training in both private & public sectors. 10 Andhra Pradesh is strongly positioned to capture this growth opportunity. It is India’s first largest egg-producing state, accounting for one-fifth of the country’s entire egg output; has one of the largest broiler (40 million) and layer (40 million) populations in the country; and enjoys 10 per cent share of total Indian broiler meat production. Because of the intensive poultry activity in the State, the supervisory and above level persons have to be well trained to have sufficient knowledgeable manpower for the poultry industry.

items.text: Poultry sector contributes Rs.145000 Cr. to National GDP and about Rs.31385 Cr. to the State’s economy. It is essential to encourage this sector not only for the sake of position but also for its efficient growth engine capabilities in rural employment generation and food security to the masses at the cheapest rate, in a short time. Andhra Pradesh stands as a leader in India's poultry industry, contributing over 18% to the nation's total egg production. In the fiscal year 2023–24, the state produced approximately 25.5 billion eggs, underscoring its robust poultry infrastructure and favorable climatic conditions. The layer chick supply facilities are more than sufficient to meet the needs of Andhra Pradesh market. Enough commercial feed milling facilities are also available with poultry farming community as well as with commercial feed manufacturing companies. Approximately, 33 Lakh tons of poultry feed is consumed every year in the state for feeding layer, broiler and breeding birds. To meet the poultry feed requirements of the state, A.P. requires 16.50 Lakh tons of coarse cereals grains like maize, jowar, ragi and by-products like rice broken and cheeru, 8.20 Lakh tons of de-oiled cakes like soybean cake, ground nut cake, cotton seed cake, rape seed cake, sunflower cake etc., and about 4.50 Lakh tons of DORB per year, all being agricultural by-products. Mineral sources like limestone grit and powder are also used to the extent of about 3.30 Lakh tons per year.

This huge consumption of agriculture products & by products by the poultry sector will greatly help agriculture farmers, rice millers, solvent extraction industries, and the mining industry in the state to market their products locally. 9.1.1. Employment opportunities through Poultry industry: One worker is required for every 2,000 poultry birds. So, poultry farming sector in the state is creating about 40,000 direct jobs in rural areas. In addition to this, thousands of jobs are also created in hatcheries and feed mills. To transport all the feed ingredients, cull birds and eggs, this sector uses about 3,000 lorries and vans every day, creating employment for about 15,000 people in 12 transport sector alone. About a million jobs are created in rural areas to raise the agricultural crops used as ingredients to produce poultry feed. Poultry farming supports the agricultural sector by using 70% of the Maize produced in the state (balance quantity of maize is used by starch and distillery industries), offering minimum support price to the maize growers, and helps the rice milling and solvent extraction industries by using their by-products like rice broken, cheeru and DORB in poultry feed, and rice husk as bedding material in deep litter poultry sheds. 9.1.2. Export Potential of Poultry Products: India is one of the countries where eggs and chicken are produced at the lowest cost. Cost of production of poultry products is also lowest in Andhra Pradesh. Therefore, export of eggs to neighboring countries of SAARC and to Middle-East countries is an opportunity which can be explored and supported by the Government.

Up-gradation of the existing and future port facilities on Andhra Pradesh Coast will facilitate Container transshipments. Dry and cold storages, with cold chain facilities, will also help to develop export of eggs and chicken meat to South East countries like Japan which is one of the highest importer of Liquid eggs and to some extent Shell eggs. In order to compete in international markets, the available genetic material in the State shall be best utilized for production of eggs and chicken meat which however shall be supported with required infrastructure for exports, freight and packing units. Trade delegations should include entrepreneurs to explore the markets abroad and understand their requirements. Facilities shall also be established at the ports for issuing necessary sanitary and phyto-sanitary certificates to facilitate exports. Air freight through ASRR International airport at Bhogapuram will also be used. 9.1.3. items.text: 9.1.4. Poultry Development in Other States: States like Maharastra, Odisha and Assam have started establishing new poultry farms recently by 13 offering subsidies, loans at lower rates of interest. There is significant raise in layer population in other states from 2015 to 2025 viz. from 29.50 lakhs to 297 lakhs in West Bengal, from 49 lakhs to 119 lakhs in Orissa and from 8.5 lakhs to 150.9 lakhs in Bihar. Poultry farmers in Andhra Pradesh are likely to face tough competition in future, to sell their products in these states, unless the Government offers similar benefits to the poultry farmers of Andhra Pradesh. 9.1.5. Agricultural Status: The poultry sector is neither treated as Industry nor agriculture for the purpose of extending incentives in the state. Some of the neighboring states have already categorized poultry as “agriculture” for the purpose of extending incentives. Andhra Pradesh should also recognize poultry as an agricultural activity immediately on par with Maharastra. 9.2.0. Broilers Andhra Pradesh has 2.88 Crore Commercial broiler birds’ capacity per crop. On an average, 5 crops of commercial broilers are reared in a year. Hence, the total number of commercial broilers raised in a year will be approximately 11 Cr. About 1.75 Lakh tons of broiler meat is produced every year. As the economic status of people gets improved, the purchasing power will also increase, thus giving a scope for further growth of about 10% in broiler sector.

As the economic status of people gets improved, the purchasing power will also increase, thus giving a scope for further growth of about 10% in broiler sector. The present per-capita consumption of chicken meat in Andhra Pradesh is 20.09 Kg’s per head per annum compared to the national average of 7.39 Kg’s as against the National Nutrition Council recommendation of 11 Kg’s. The per-capita consumption in Andhra Pradesh is too low when compared to Brazil and America where it is more than 46 Kg’s. In Japan, it is 14.7 Kg’s. Chicken produced in Andhra Pradesh state also caters to the needs of neighboring districts of Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka States. Most of the broiler chick requirement is met from hatcheries located in Telangana State, due to the fact that most of the broiler breeder farms and hatcheries are located in and around Hyderabad area of combined state. 14 Chicken meat is also a rich source of protein in the form of healthy white meat which helps to solve the protein malnutrition problem. It has the highest protein content among all other meats and is available at about half of the mutton price. Unlike other meats, chicken meat production can be achieved in shortest possible time and it has no cultural or religious barriers. Beef and pork will not be consumed by all religious groups. In India, majority of the consumers prefer chicken dressed in front of the consumer. Consumers dislike chilled & packed meat. Wet bird market (live bird market) is more than 95% in India.

Wet bird market (live bird market) is more than 95% in India. This result in unsanitary conditions at chicken centers, improper disposal of dressing waste raises public health issues. Street slaughter has to be regulated. Awareness has to be created regarding advantages of mechanized slaughter, chilled and packed meat where manual handling is less, with ante-mortem and post- mortem inspection, with which the meat quality will be good with known microbial load. In Andhra Pradesh, 70-75 % broiler farmers are in integration system and the remaining are non - integrators. Integrators will supply chick, feed and medicines etc., whereas the farmer has to prepare shed and meet electricity & labor expenses by himself. At marketing stage, farmer will be paid based on live weights obtained. Whether an individual farmer or integrator, the chain ends with live birds marketing which is called horizontal integration. However, vertical integration needs to be developed, where live birds are dressed in processing plant and value addition is done. Chicken processing and value addition are the other areas yet to catch up in Andhra Pradesh. Though the processing sector is limited today, this will gradually increase as the per-capita income increases due to urbanization. 9.3.0. The Eggs & Meat produced from the Desi birds are having high commercial demand and good source of easily available protein supplements to the rural livelihoods. 15 Establishment of 2720 Mother Poultry Units through SHGs in the next five years in Andhra Pradesh with Capacity building and technical support by the Animal Husbandry Department with 50% subsidy per unit. Through this support, Mother Poultry Units will be able to procure essential infrastructure such as brooders, feeders, waterers, electricity backup, bio security measures, and quality parent stock. These mother poultry units will inturn supply quality Chicks and inputs to interested backyard poultry farmers in villages. 10.0 ROLE OF STATE ANIMAL HUSBANDRY DEPARTMENT IN POULTRY SECTOR Present scenario of Animal Husbandry Department with the Commercial Poultry is that, there is no involvement of State Animal Husbandry Department in any step of Commercial poultry establishment & rearing activity. The Commercial poultry farms are approaching the AH Department during the natural calamities, while seeking compensation and during poultry products sale crises only. Further, Poultry Farms Registration in the state is very important in the view of recent Avian Influenza Outbreaks in the state and across the Country. Poultry Farms Registration is also important for implementation of strict Bio Security measures wherein Poultry Farms must enhance hygienic practices, control farm access and follow stringent Bio-Security protocols to minimize the risk of infection, strengthened Surveillance, Solid waste management and mandatory Registration of all Poultry Farms to enhance disease tracking and control. 10.1. items.text: 10.1. A.P. State Poultry farms Registration In this policy it is proposed to mandatorily register all Poultry farms in A.P. State and their activities connected with poultry farming and traceability matters concerned there with or incidental thereto and to make available healthy and disease free poultry meat, eggs and live birds to public at large for human consumption. All poultry farms must register with AP State Animal Husbandry Departments to ascertain traceability of the farm location, inputs, outputs etc. The Government of India has urged Poultry industry stake holders to 16 ensure 100% compliance with this directive. All Government Poultry farms shall be registered on free of cost. The involvement of State Animal Husbandry Department must be as mentioned below: 10.1.1 Registration with AH Department: (Commercial Poultry, Egg traders & packers) A) Commercial Poultry:  All the Commercial Poultry farms (Layers/Broilers) shall be registered mandatory with the Animal Husbandry Department along with other permission protocols presently followed in vogue and it should be mandatory.  Classification of Poultry Farms: Backyard poultry is typically owned by small and marginal farmer and comprises of few birds, largely for self- consumption and very small quantities get commercially sold. The poultry farming practiced by the rural and tribal farmers under free range or backyard or semi-intensive systems is usually referred to as rural poultry farming.  Based on the number of handling of birds, Poultry farms may be classified as per para 10.1.3.

items.text: 10.1.6 Poultry - Public Health Measures:  No person shall feed or cause to feed Growth Hormones, Phosphates, Pig Fat to poultry birds through feed, water or any other means.  No person shall inject or cause to inject Growth Hormones to Poultry birds.  Only in case of disease conditions where Antibiotic therapy is required, the poultry birds will be permitted to be fed with Antibiotics in prescribed doses after obtaining prescription from Registered Veterinary Practitioner and under his / her supervision.  The Poultry birds treated with Antibiotics should not be sold in the market for human consumption prior to completion of a period of minimum 7 days or for the period as prescribed in the literature of specific Antibiotic from the date of stoppage of the course of Antibiotics.  If the poultry birds are under the treatment of Veterinarian, no person shall sale or cause to sale the poultry birds for human consumption before the completion of drug withdrawal period or as prescribed by the Veterinarian.  If found necessary, the poultry farm owner can take the advice and obtain prescription of Registered Veterinary Practitioner for treatment of the poultry birds.  Analysis of Drinking Water in Commercial Poultry Farms: The analysis of drinking water in commercial poultry farms is crucial for ensuring the health of poultry birds and optimizing production efficiency. The Animal Husbandry Department will have facility of analysis of drinking water 20 used in the poultry farms at Veterinary Biological Research Institute (VBRI) Vijayawada and the guidelines are appended in the Annexure VII.

The Andhra Pradesh Food Processing Policy 2024-29 is designed with a core focus on value addition as the key driver for growth across the Agriculture, Horticulture, Aqua, and Animal Husbandry sectors. By treating all sectors with equal importance, the policy aims to create a balanced ecosystem that encourages innovation and processing at every level of the value chain. The primary objective is to transform raw produce into higher- value products, thereby boosting market competitiveness, enhancing export 23 potential, and increasing profitability for farmers and entrepreneurs alike. This strong livestock base is crucial for the development of downstream processing industries, such as dairy and meat processing, and plays a key role in rural employment and income generation. 11.1.1 Product Perfection, Cluster Development, Storage and Value Addition (Clause 3.2.2) The Government of Andhra Pradesh will adopt a commodity based cluster development approach to strategically enhance the food processing industry. This cluster-based strategy focuses on leveraging the proximity of raw material sources and maximizing the use of shared processing infrastructure to seamlessly integrate production hubs with processing centers. As per the Andhra Pradesh Processing Policy 4.0 (2024-29) (1.2.2) high potential areas for poultry sector are identified at East Godavari, Prakasam, Chittoor, Krishna, Guntur, West Godavari, Annamayya, Eluru districts and in these clusters will drive efficient resource utilization, reduce post-harvest losses, and attract targeted investments.

The rate of interest subvention will be allowed by the technical committee 30 report of the AH Department basing on prevailing Marginal Cost of Funds- based Lending Rate (MCLR) every year. Under this scheme, eligible poultry farms will receive a subsidy on the interest portion of their loans, effectively reducing their borrowing costs. This financial relief aims to ease the burden of high input costs, especially during challenging periods such as disease outbreaks or price volatility, and to encourage continued production and modernization. The subvention will be linked to Marginal Cost of Funds based on Lending Rates (MCLR) to ensure transparency and alignment with current market rates. Every year, the rate of interest subvention will be permitted as per the recommendation of the Animal Husbandry Department, ensuring it remains relevant to the sector's financial needs and economic conditions.

items.text: Every year, the rate of interest subvention will be permitted as per the recommendation of the Animal Husbandry Department, ensuring it remains relevant to the sector's financial needs and economic conditions. Hence, to ease the financial burden and encourage growth in the poultry sector, the Animal Husbandry Department is proposing an Interest Subvention Scheme for poultry farmers availing bank loans of existing and newly establishing farms basing on prevailing Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate (MCLR). The key features of the scheme are: 1. Objective: To reduce the effective interest rate on loans taken by poultry farmers for working capital, infrastructure, and expansion. 2. Eligibility: All poultry farmers for both existing & newly establishing (broiler, layer, back yard) with valid unit registration and bank loan accounts. 3. Loan Coverage: Term loans and working capital loans taken from scheduled commercial banks, cooperative banks, and RRBs. 4. Subvention Details: State Government will reimburse a portion of the interest rate basing on average of MCLR of commercial banks every year and the Animal Husbandry Department will propose the rate of interest subvention to the Government, reducing the effective interest paid by the farmer. Applicable for prompt repayment accounts as per bank norms. 5. Implementation & Disbursement: Interest subvention will be disbursed directly to the bank account by reimbursement process to the poultry 31 farmer annually. Animal Husbandry Department will act as the nodal agency by taking help of Andhra Pradesh Poultry Federation (APPF).

Local egg consumption will be increased. d. Poultry meat consumption will be increased, more number of poultry farms will be established and egg production will be increased. e. Supplementary income and nutrition to the BPL families. f. Additional employment opportunities to rural youth. Converting BPL families to Lakpathi didids. g. Support prices to Maize producing farmers. h. Reduction in malnutrition and protein deficiency in children. i. Export potential of eggs and egg powder to other countries will be possible.

Date: Authorized Signatory Name: Designation: 53 Seal/Stamp: Annexure – VII Guidelines for Drinking Water Testing in Poultry Farms Ensuring high-quality drinking water is vital in poultry farming, as water is a primary vector for disease transmission and a critical route for medication and vaccination. Routine testing and corrective actions help maintain flock health, optimize productivity, and protect public health. 1. Frequency of Testing  Water quality in commercial poultry farms should be tested at least once annually; twice a year is ideal.  Immediate testing is advised if there are changes in water color, taste, odor, or signs of poor bird performance or health. 2. Parameters to be analyzed I. Chemical Parameters The following chemical indicators are crucial: pH Optimal range: 6.5–8.5. Influences vaccine efficacy and bird digestion. Total Hardness Excessive calcium/magnesium can clog drinkers and interfere with digestion. Chlorides High levels give salty or bitter taste; may lead to diarrhea and reduced intake. Sulphates Cause diarrhea, stunted growth, and corrosion of equipment.

items.text: Total Hardness Excessive calcium/magnesium can clog drinkers and interfere with digestion. Chlorides High levels give salty or bitter taste; may lead to diarrhea and reduced intake. Sulphates Cause diarrhea, stunted growth, and corrosion of equipment. Nitrates/Nitrites Indicators of organic contamination; toxic at high levels, causing cyanosis, stunted growth, and death. Arsenic Cumulative toxin from soil or pesticides; affects multiple organ systems and poses public health risks. Calcium & Magnesium Influence hardness and taste; excess magnesium sulfate causes diarrhea. 54 Bicarbonates/ Carbonates Contribute to alkalinity; generally beneficial. Ammonium Marker of contamination from waste or bacteria. Standard acceptable limits should be referred from BIS/ICAR guidelines. II. Microbiological Parameters Contamination by microorganisms can lead to significant flock mortality and reduced productivity. Common pathogens:  Salmonella spp., Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas spp., Vibrio cholerae, Leptospira spp.  Protozoa, helminth eggs, and fungi may also be present. Testing should cover:  Source water  Drinking points (nipples, cups)  Overhead tanks and storage 3. Methods to Improve Water Quality A. Microbiological Quality Method Description Chlorination Common, cost-effective; manual or automatic; requires dose verification. Acidification Organic/inorganic acids lower pH to reduce microbial growth. Botanical Extracts E.g., Cimenol ring—plant-based, eco-friendly biocidal agents. Facility Hygiene Proper materials and regular cleaning reduce biofilm formation and microbial load. B.

Facility Hygiene Proper materials and regular cleaning reduce biofilm formation and microbial load. B. Chemical Quality Method Application Reverse Osmosis (RO) Eliminates excess solutes and contaminants. Filtration Removes suspended solids; depends on filter type. Flocculation Coagulants like aluminum/iron salts remove heavy metals and suspended particles. 4. Conclusion Water serves not just for hydration but as a vehicle for treatment during illness. Birds continue to drink even when feed intake drops, making water quality a direct factor in treatment efficacy. 55 Key outcomes of good water management: Better bird health, Higher productivity, Lower mortality and treatment costs and Sustainable farm operation. Minutes of the Meeting with all Food Secretaries of DCP states by the Secretary, DFPD,GoI, New Delhi Dated:19,09,2025 *** 1. Levy System: Rice required for Public Distribution and Other Welfare Schemes was procured through mill levy from the Rice Millers as per the AP Rice Procurement (levy) Order,1984. Levy system was continued up to KMS 2014,15. 2. Decentralized Procurement System: Decentralized Procurement (DCP) has been taken up in the State w. e.f. 1 st October 2015 to ensure payment of Minimum Support P rice (MSP) for paddy to the farmers and to avoid exploit ation of farmers by any intermediaries and acquire self,suff iciency in procuring rice for Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) and Other Welfare Schemes (OWS) in the state. 3. MoU with Government of India: A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was executed with the Governmen t of India on Decentralized Procurement (DCP) Scheme.

items.text: 3. MoU with Government of India: A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was executed with the Governmen t of India on Decentralized Procurement (DCP) Scheme. As per the DCP scheme the State Government / its agencies shall procure paddy from the farmers, custom mill the pad dy and 2 retain the resultant raw rice to the extent require d for TPDS and OWS as per allocation made by the Central Gover nment and handover the excess stocks to the Food Corporat ion of India (FCI) for central pool operations. 4. Govt. of AP has been taking several initiatives to benefit the farmers. In this context, Government has constitute d a Group of Ministers (GoM) to suggest measures for improvement of paddy procurement process. The GoM h as recommended the following measures for improvement of the Paddy procurement operations: a. All necessary steps shall be taken to ensure paymen t of 100% MSP to farmers. b. Paddy Procurement Centers (PPCs) shall be established at all Paddy growing districts across the State for the easy access of the farmers. Procurement Support Agencies (PSAs) shall be engaged to run the paddy procurement operations by PPCs at RSKs. c. Integration with Agriculture Department: Procurement of paddy shall be done on the basis of e,Panta data of Agriculture Department. All paddy growing farmers (including tenants)shall be registered in e,Panta portal by Rythu Sahaya Kendras Assistants before commencement of paddy procurement. d. If quality of paddy is in adherence to Fair Average Quality (FAQ) norms, paddy shall be procured immediately.

It shall be mandatory that the Rice Miller s return CMR within three months of receipt of paddy stock b ut not later than prescribed time limit of Government of India. 8. Sortex and Blending Facilities : Paddy shall be allotted to the Rice Millers having Sortex and Fortified Rice K ernel Blending machinery only. Each Rice Miller shall get +F endorsement from FSSAI to mark +F symbol in blue co lour on CMR gunny bag and rexin slip. 15. Fortification of Rice: All the rice millers shall install FRK dynamic blending machinery which is weight based fo r blending of fortified rice kernels with CMR during custom milling stage in 1:100 ratio, as per the GOI guidel ines. They should get registered in the Fortrace portal and up load the CoA accordingly. The availability of blending facil ity for fortified rice in every rice mill is mandatory. The implementation of the Fortified Rice Kernel Managem ent System (FRQMS) is mandated for all FRK production a nd distribution activities. Capturing of the Bio,metrics of farmers/nominee of farmers during paddy procurement. 2. Tracking of the Electricity Consumption of the Rice Mills. 3. Tracking of the Paddy and CMR Transportation Vehicl es from loading point (Farmgate/RSK) to unloading poin t (Rice Mills) and rice from mills to godowns. Joint Collectors should implement the above New Minimum Threshold Parameters duly tracking of the electrici ty consumption of the Rice Mills and submission of the ATRs and Tracking of the paddy and CMR transportation vehicles through GPS devices. 19. All the raw rice consignments shall be subjected to another test i.e., mixed indicator method for determination of age of milled raw rice stocks. Quality of Gunnies: The custodian officer shall be held equally responsible as the rice miller concerned ab out the quality of gunnies being supplied to PPCs or Mandal Level Godowns by the respective rice millers. Random qual ity checks of the once used gunny bags supplied for sto ring paddy shall be conducted by the Revenue / Civil Sup plies staff or whosoever is assigned for this task by the district procurement authorities at the mill point before dispatch by the PSA staff after their delivery at respective RS K/Mandal Level Godown. In case, the Rice Miller is providing gunny bags to the PPCs, the miller shall ensure clear identification of the rice mill like mill code or number unique to Rice Mill is present on each gunny bag. 34. Recycling of PDS Rice and other Unfair Trade Practi ces : The Rice Millers shall not purchase and recycle the PDS rice for delivery as Custom Milled Rice (CMR). CMR shall not be used or cause to be used for sale in the open marke t in the guise of non PDS rice/super fine rice or export to the other countries either by reconditioning or changing the bags, etc., Violation of this condition shall attract the meaning of Mischief under Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya S anhita (BNS) and the miller shall be liable for criminal a ction by imposing Prevention of Damage to Public Property Ac t, 1984, and Andhra Pradesh Revenue Recovery Act, 1864 , to recover the CMR dues equivalent penal value besides black listing for FIVE years. Bank Guarantee will be forf eited if any mill found to engage in offences like recycling.

Enforcement Activities : The District Collectors shall ensure that the enforcement officials and any other teams 9 constituted for the purpose of monitoring paddy procurement and milling operations shall inspect th e rice mills periodically to ensure that the paddy handed over for custom milling is stored under proper conditions, a nd other aspects such as milling of paddy, delivery of CMR, balance stock available etc., and to take immediate action if any discrepancy is noticed. If any shortage in stocks i s found, the miller is liable to pay one and half time (1 ½) the value of CMR in shortage and also liable for criminal act ion for criminal breach of trust and misappropriation of Go vt. stocks under Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya San hita (BNS). 36. Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) was repl aced by Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) on July 1, 2024. items.text: Criteria for categorization and random selection of Mills for JPV a. The exercise for categorization and selection of mi lls has been structured to ensure a random and impartia l process, driven by system,generated data, thereby eliminating discretion and enhancing transparency. b. The selection of 10% mills for JPV will be based on the quantity of un,milled paddy available with each mil l as reflected in the CFPP/relevant module and CFSP. Therefore, it is essential that data on CFPP and CF SP is accurately updated before any application for extension is submitted. The selection criteria are detailed below. c. All mills/storage points having un,milled paddy in a revenue district will be arranged in descending ord er of the quantity of un,milled paddy. The list will b e further categorized into three parts, as below: Category,A: Top 30% of mills/storage points in the list Category,B: Between 30% to 60% of mills/storage points in the list Category,C: Remaining 40% of the mills/storage points in the list d. It will be ensured that 6%, 3% and 1% of the total number of mills/storage points are randomly selecte d for JPV from Category , A, B and C, respectively, subject to a minimum of one (1) mill/storage point from each category. In case of total number of such 20 mills/storage points being 3 or less, JPV is to be carried out in all the mills/storage points. e.

items.text: Levy system was continued up to KMS 2014-15. 2. Decentralized Procurement System: Decentralized Procurement (DCP) has been taken up in the State w.e.f. 1 st October 2015 to ensure payment of Minimum Support Price (MSP) for paddy to the farmers and to avoid exploitation of farmers by any intermediaries and acquire self -sufficiency in procuring rice for Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) and Other Welfare Schemes (OWS) in the state. 3. MoU with Government of India: A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was executed with the Government of India on Decentralized Procurement (DCP) Scheme. As per the DCP scheme the State Government / its agencies shall procure paddy from the farmers, custom mill the paddy and retain the resultant raw rice to the extent required for TPDS and OWS a s per allocation made by the Central Government and handover the excess stocks to the Food Corporation of India ( FCI) for central pool operations. 4. Govt. of AP has been taking several initiatives to benefit the farmers. In this context, Government has constituted a Group of Ministers (GoM) to suggest measures for improvement of paddy procurement process. The GoM has recommended the following measures for improvement of the Paddy procurement operations: a. All necessary steps shall be taken to ensure paym ent of 100% MSP to farmers. b. Paddy Procurement Centers (PPCs) shall be established at all Paddy growing districts across the State for the easy access of the farmers. Procurement Support Agencies (PSAs) shall be engaged to run the paddy procurement operations by PPCs at RSKs. c. Integration with Agriculture Department:

items.text: Paddy Procurement Centers (PPCs) shall be established at all Paddy growing districts across the State for the easy access of the farmers. Procurement Support Agencies (PSAs) shall be engaged to run the paddy procurement operations by PPCs at RSKs. c. Integration with Agriculture Department: Procurement of paddy shall be done on the basis of e-Panta data of Agriculture Department. All paddy growing farmers (including tenant s) shall be registered in e-Panta portal by Rythu Sahaya Kendras Assistants before commencement of paddy procurement. Procurement will be done to the farmers having Farmer Id registered in e -Panta portal. d. If quality of paddy is in adherence to F air Average Quality (FAQ) norms, paddy shall be procured immediately. If paddy quality is not in conformity with FAQ norms, technical staff shall sensitize and request farmers to bring the paddy within the FAQ norms by drying and cleaning etc. e. Aadhar based payment shall be made to farmers based on e-Panta data shared by Agriculture Department. 5. State Level Procurement Agencies: The A ndhra Pradesh State Civil Supplies Corporation Limited (A PSCSCL) and Andhra Pradesh State Co -operative Marketing Federation Ltd. ( AP MARKFED) shall function as State Level Procurement Agencies for the season KMS 2026-27. AP MARKFED is appointed as an additional agency for paddy procurement fo r KMS 202 6- 27(G.O.Rt.No.42, CAF & CS (CS -II) Department dated:05.10.2026). The AP MARKFED in association with the APSCSCL would be responsible for the paddy procurement operations in the entire State of Andhra Pradesh.

items.text: The AP MARKFED in association with the APSCSCL would be responsible for the paddy procurement operations in the entire State of Andhra Pradesh. APSCSCL shall be responsible for custom milling and distribution of Rice under various schemes. 6. District Procurement Committee : District Collectors shall constitute a District Procurement Committee with the Joint Collector as Chairman with District Level Officials of all connected departments, namely Agriculture, Marketing, Cooperative, Civil Supplies, Transport, Rural Development (DRDA), Tribal Welfare ( ITDA), I&PR, Warehousing Agencies (CWC, SWC), Procurement Agencies (FCI, APSCSCL) and also Sub-Collectors/RDOs as members to coordinate and decide on all the activities and monitor the procurement related activities on a day-to-day basis. 7. Custom Milling and delivery of Custom Milled Rice (CMR): The Rice Millers shall commence milling of paddy received from the PPCs within a week from the date and time of receipt and shall complete custom milling of paddy and deliver the resultant rice either as raw rice or boiled rice to the FC I and Raw Rice to APSCSCL within time frame prescribed by the Government or the APSCSCL for the paddy handed over by the APSCSCL/AP MARKFED. It shall be mandatory that the Rice Millers return CMR within three months of receipt of paddy stock but not later than prescribed time limit of Go vernment of India. (No. 1(6)/2023-Py.I, Government of India Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution Department of Food & Pu blic Distribution Dated:13 -08- 2024) 8.

APSCSCL shall maintain truck wise paddy issue entries and monitor them for receipt of proportionate CMR within the permitted time. 9. Paddy Procurement Portal: All Rice Millers engaged for paddy procurement operations should be mandatorily registered on the AP Paddy Procurement Portal. 10. Self-certification and physical assessment : Rice Mills designated for milling within the State shall be registered online only after self-certification by the rice mills and physical assessment of their infrastructure and installed capacit ies by the Inspecting Officer appointed by the JC & EOED. 11. Custom Milling Operations: The Rice Millers shall undertake custom milling of paddy procured by the State Government / its Agencies (APSCSCL & AP MARKFFED), as per the agreed terms and conditions and at the rates and norms fixed by the Government of India. 12. Allocation of Paddy for Custom Milling: The allocation of paddy to mills for custom milling shall be made only up to 75% of their milling capacity, by considering a period of three months in a season (Kharif/Rabi), as per the instructions of the Government of India. The allocation of paddy targets shall be finalized in consultation with the concerned District Rice Millers Association, ensuring uniformity, transparency and fairness among all rice millers in the district.

items.text: The allocation of paddy targets shall be finalized in consultation with the concerned District Rice Millers Association, ensuring uniformity, transparency and fairness among all rice millers in the district. While fixing the individual targets, uniform parameters shall be followed, duly considering the actual available milli ng capacity, milling infrastructure, machinery, storage and other related facilities of each rice mill, along with the total quantity of paddy available and required to be milled in the district. In case any discrepancy or difference of opinion is noticed in the allocation of targets, the matter shall be referred to the concerned Joint Collector, whose decision shall be final. 13. Allocation of Rice Mill targets: Systematic assessment of the performance of rice mills in respect of delivery of Custom Milled Rice (CMR) during Kharif and Rabi 2025 –26. Undertake a comprehensive review of the performance of each rice mill with reference to the following parameters. Sl. No. Parameter Key aspects to be assessed 1 Past CMR Delivery Performance Paddy allotted; CMR to be delivered; CMR delivered; percentage delivered within milling period; pending CMR; average delay; performance in both Kharif and Rabi 2025–26 2 Quality Performance Number/percentage of rejections; BRL stocks; repeated non-conforming supplies; timely replacement of rejected stocks; adherence to Raw/Boiled/Fine/Improved CMR specifications 3 Milling Capacity & Infrastructure Installed milling capacity; actual operational capacity; Sortex facility; Dryers, storage space; weighbridge; calibrated moisture meter;

Electronic Bank Guarantee : Paddy shall be allotted to the rice mills for custom milling and delivery of CMR strictly as mentioned above. The District Civil Supplies Manager (DCSM), APSCSCL shall enter MOU with the designated rice mills in the prescribed format duly collecting e-Bank Guarantees in the prescribed ratio.

The District Civil Supplies Manager (DCSM), APSCSCL shall enter MOU with the designated rice mills in the prescribed format duly collecting e-Bank Guarantees in the prescribed ratio. The Bank Guarantee shall be submitted in the electronic format only as e-BG (Electronic Bank Guarantee) so that it is integrated with the paddy procurement portal for validation. Based on the ownership status and su bmission of Cluster Agreement (Annexure-V), the system shall clearly categorize the rice mills and determine the required Bank Guarantee coverage 15. The miller undertakes to keep the bank guarantee valid till the completion of CMR Rice delivery to CSC/FCI an d resultant brokens to the successful bidder/FCI/CSC fully. 16. Custom Milling Agreements – Execution by APSCSCL for and on behalf of the State Government: The paddy procured under the De -Centralized Procurement Scheme is procured by the State Government through its agencies, out of funds provided and arranged by the Government, and the resultant Custom Milled Rice is taken over for the Targeted Public Distribution System and Other Welfare Schemes, which is a function entrusted to a Panchayat under Article 243G and to a Municipality under Article 243W of the Constitution of India. The custom milling of such paddy by the rice millers is, in substance, a service rendered to the State Government, the APSCSCL and AP MARKFED acting as the implementing and nominated agencies of the Government. Government accordingly order as follows: i. The agreement for storage and custom milling of paddy into raw/boiled rice shall be entered into by the Government of Andhra Pradesh, acting through and represented by the APSCSCL. T he District Civil Supplies Manager, APSCSCL of the district concerned is hereby authorised to sign and execute the said agreement with the rice millers for and on behalf of the Government of Andhra Pradesh. ii. The APSCSCL shall sign, execute, administer, implement, process, monitor and enforce the said agreements, and do all acts, deeds and things required thereunder, solely in its representative capacity as the authorised agency of the Government of Andhra Pradesh, and not as a principal contracting party in its own right. iii. Every right, power, discretion, approval, decision, direction, allotment, inspection, payment, deduction, recovery, set -off, levy of penalty, invocation of Bank Guarantee, blacklisting, termination and foreclosure exercised under the sa id agreements by the APSCSCL or any of its officers, including the VC & Managing Director, the Joint Collector & Ex-Officio Executive Director and the District Civil Supplies Manager, shall be deemed to be exercised for and on behalf of the Government of A ndhra Pradesh. iv.

items.text: The paddy, rice, gunny bags, Fortified Rice Kernels and other stocks handed over to the rice millers under the said agreements are the property of the Government, held and dealt with by the APSCSCL for and on behalf of the Government; and t he Bank Guarantees, security deposits, penalties and other amounts furnished to, received or recovered by the APSCSCL under the said agreements are so furnished, received or recovered by it for and on behalf of the Government. v. All suits, arbitrations, cla ims, appeals and other legal proceedings arising out of or in connection with the said agreements shall be instituted, prosecuted and defended by or against the APSCSCL only in its representative capacity for and on behalf of the Government of Andhra Pradesh, and the APSCSCL shall be so described in every such proceeding. vi. The milling charges, driage charges, custody and maintenance charges, sortex and improved specification charges, gunny user charges and transportation charges payable under the said agree ments at the rates fixed by the Government of India and by the State Level Committee constitute the consideration paid by the Government of Andhra Pradesh for the milling services rendered to it, and the rates and other commercial terms applicable to the r ice millers remain unaltered by these orders. 17. The APSCSCL is directed to capture Geo-Coordinates of the defaulted rice mill premises for the past years and the same rice mill premises is blocked for participation in the CMR operations until dues including penalty to APSCSCL is cleared. 20. As per the instructions of the Government of India to implement the following New Minimum Threshold Parameters. 1. Capturing of the Bio -metrics of farmers/nominee of farmers during paddy procurement. 2. Tracking of the Electricity Consumption of the Rice Mills. 3. Tracking of the Paddy and CMR Transportation Vehicles from loading point (Farmgate/RSK) to unloading point (Rice Mills) and rice from mills to godowns. Joint Collectors should imp lement the above New Minimum Threshold Parameters duly tracking of the electricity consumption of the Rice Mills and submission of the ATRs and Tracking of the paddy and CMR transportation vehicles through GPS devices. 21. All the raw rice consignments shall be subjected to another test i.e., mixed indicator method for determination of age of milled raw rice stocks. As per the instructions in vogue, a sample shall be drawn from the offered consignment and analyzed in terms of FAQ specifications of GoI. If it is found conforming to the prescribed specifications, the samples would be tested through mixed indicator method.

items.text: As per the instructions in vogue, a sample shall be drawn from the offered consignment and analyzed in terms of FAQ specifications of GoI. If it is found conforming to the prescribed specifications, the samples would be tested through mixed indicator method. In case the color of the reagent comes out to be green/avocado green, the consignment would be accepted and any other color like yellow, yellow orange & orange would be rejected terming the stock as 'Not freshly Milled'. 22. Non-trading rice mills shall only be given paddy allocation in the usual circumstances. (No. 1(6)/2023-Py.I, Government of India Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution Department of Food & Public Distribution Dated:13-08-2024) 23. Trading rice mills should be given paddy only as a last resort if there are no non-trading mills with prior permission of VC&MD, APSCSCL. In that case, the trading rice mill should maintain separate registers and accounts, and preferably separate storage f or privately purchased paddy/rice, State Pool paddy/CMR and Central pool paddy/CMR shall be stored in a countable manner. (No. 1(6)/2023 -Py.I, Government of India Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution Department of Food & Public Distribu tion Dated:13-08-2024) 24. Trading Rice Mills shall not be allowed to mill/process privately purchased paddy and its products until completion of CMR delivery to APSCSCL/FCI unless they have separate Milling Units under one firm with separate Electricity Serv ice connections.

items.text: Trading Rice Mills shall not be allowed to mill/process privately purchased paddy and its products until completion of CMR delivery to APSCSCL/FCI unless they have separate Milling Units under one firm with separate Electricity Serv ice connections. 25. The rice mills which are trading rice/ broken rice in their rice mill privately should not be considered at any circumstances for custom milling operations. 26. Tagging of Rice Mills to RSKs : The district procurement authorities shall tag the PPCs at RSKs for shifting of paddy procured to the nearest rice mills to the extent possible. However, the farmer shall have liberty to choose the rice mill for paddy procurement subject to ceiling on payment of paddy transport charges to the lowest ap plicable slab in that area as per slab system (0-8 Kms, 9-20 Kms, 21-40 Kms, 41-80 Kms, above 80 Kms). If any mill tagged beyond 40 KMs, the transportation charges beyond 40 KMs shall be borne by the Farmer/Appointed Transport Contractor/Agency or any othe r transporter engaged as paddy transporter only. The tagging beyond 40 Kms must be done with proper justification only. 27. Electricity Consumption: The milling capacity should be corroborated with the average electricity consumption for the full year of KMS 2025-26. The monthly electricity consumption data for KMS 202 5-26 shall be integrated in the AP Paddy Procurement Portal by linking it with DISCOMs such as EPDCL, CPDCL & SPDCL so that real time information is available on the paddy milled vs. electricity consumed. The same data shall be used for transmission to Central Food Procurement Portal (CFPP). 28.

Blacklisting of Rice Mills for discrepancies in electricity consumption: The Rice mills who are found with discrepancies in electricity consumption shall be duly blacklisted from custom milling with APSCSCL. They shall not be allowed to participate in the CMR operations for FIVE YEARS besides taking other punitive action. 29. Minimum Support Price: The Minimum Support Prices (MSP) for FAQ paddy fixed by Government of India for the KMS 202 6- 27 (Kharif and Rabi) are as follows. 1. Common: Rs.2,441/- per quintal. 2. Grade-A Rs.2,461/- per quintal. 30. Uniform Specifications for Paddy and Rice : The Uniform specifications for paddy and rice fixed by the Government of India are detailed in Annexure-I,II& III. 31. Open Market Purchase Operations : The rice millers may also purchase FAQ paddy at a price not less than the MSP and they shall invariably make payment to the farmers directly to the bank accounts of farmers through NEFT/RTGS or A/c payee cheques. 32. Maintenance of A and B Registers: The rice millers shall maintain the details of paddy purchased, rice produced, sold, balance stock available in the mills etc., duly computerized in real time in form ‘A’ and ‘B’ registers prescribed in the A.P. Online Updation of A and B Registers: The millers shall mandatorily update the A & B Registers in the paddy procurement portal on daily basis and make all information available online for verific ation. Failure to update such information online in the paddy procurement portal shall attract penal provisions and non -payment of milling charges for CMR rice. 34. Supply of Gunnies by Rice Mills for Paddy Procurement: Paddy allotment quantity for custom milling shall be linked with milling capacity of the mill which will be subjected to the pre-condition that the miller is duty bound to supply proportionate number of good quality/sound once used gunnies in advance at the localities specified by district procurement authorities. The District Rice Millers association shall be responsible for mobilizing the good quality of Gunnies from the Rice Mills and monitor the positioning of the gunnies at designated locations. Non -supply or not supplying the gunnies in time will automatically result in reduction of the custom milling paddy target and further action of barring such mills from custom milling operations. Atleast the gunnies required for 30% of allotted target shall be positioned by Rice miller in advance at tagged PPCs at RSKs in order to generate first truck chit. 35. Quality of Gunnies: The custodian officer shall be held equally responsible as the rice miller concerned about the quality of gunnies being supplied to PPCs or Mandal Level Godowns by the respective rice millers.

The above three Rice Mills shall constitute one Cluster for KMS 2026 –27 and this single Agreement shall be sufficient for all the three Rice Mills forming the Cluster. b. Each Cluster Member shall act as a reciprocal Co -Guarantor for the other two Cluster Members, and the obligations contained in this Agr eement shall apply mutually and equally to all the three Rice Mills. c. No Rice Mill forming part of this Cluster shall be permitted to become a member, guarantor or co -guarantor of any other Cluster during the same procurement season. d. The constitution of the Cluster shall be recorded in the Paddy Procurement Portal, and once the Cluster Agreement is accepted and paddy is allotted, no Cluster Member shall withdraw, substitute itself or join any other Cluster without the prior written approval of the competent authority. e. Any reconstitution of the Cluster shall be permitted only after ensuring that the Government's financial and CMR interests are fully safeguarded and the prescribed e-BG requirements are fulfilled. 2. Electronic Bank Guarantees: Each Cluster Member shall independently furnish a. Valid Electronic Bank Guarantee (e -BG) in accordance with its ownership status and the applicable Government Orders / SoP for KMS 2026–27. b. The applicable e -BG coverage for Rice Mills submitting this Cluster Agreement shall be:  Own Rice Mill + Cluster Agreement – Paddy Value : BG Value = 1:1  Leased Rice Mill + Cluster Agreement – Paddy Value : BG Value = 1:1.5 c.

In the case of a leased Rice Mill, a valid lease document covering the entire Agreement period shall also be furnished. d. No paddy shall be allotted beyond the quantity eligible against the valid e - BG available to the respective Rice Mill in the Paddy Procurement Portal. e. All e -BGs furnished by the Cluster Members shall remain valid and enforceable for the prescribe d period and until discharge of the CMR including disposal of resultant brokens and financial obligations secured thereunder, including the extended period wherever applicable. 3. Joint and Several Responsibility for CMR: a. The three Cluster Members hereby jo intly undertake to safeguard the entire Paddy received from Paddy Procurement Centres, entrusted to the Rice Mills forming the Cluster and to ensure timely milling and delivery of the entire CMR due to APSCSCL/FCI within the stipulated period and in accordance with the prescribed quality specifications. b. Though paddy may be allotted separately to each Rice Mill, all the three Cluster Members shall be jointly and severally responsible for ensuring fulfilment of the CMR obligations of every Rice Mill forming part of the Cluster. c. The Rice Mill to which Paddy is physically entrusted shall continue to have primary responsibility for safe custody, accounting, milling and delivery of CMR against such paddy. The joint responsibility of the other Cluster Members sha ll be in addition to, and shall not dilute, the primary responsibility of the concerned Rice Mill. d.

items.text: The joint responsibility of the other Cluster Members sha ll be in addition to, and shall not dilute, the primary responsibility of the concerned Rice Mill. d. In the event of delay or default by any one Cluster Member, the other two Cluster Members shall cooperate with APSCSCL and ensure that the outstanding CMR obligation / consequential financial liability is made good in accordance with the directions of the competent authority and the applicable Government Orders, SoP and Agreement conditions. e. No transfer of Government paddy or CMR from one Cluster Member's premises to another Cluster Member's premises shall be made without prior written permission of the competent authority. 4. Liability in Case of Default: a. The following, among others, shall constitute default under this Agreement:  Failure to deliver CMR within the stipulated period;  Shortage or non-availability of paddy/CMR during inspection;  Non-accounting or misappropriation of Government stocks;  Unauthorized sale, diversion, transfer or disposal of paddy;  Recycling/substitution of PDS rice;  Delivery of rice from an unauthorized source;  Failure to comply with the Government Orders, SoP or Rice Miller Agreement resulting in financial loss to the Government/Corporation. b. In the event of default by any Cluster Member, the liability of the defaulting Rice Mill sha ll first be determined in accordance with the applicable Government Orders, SoP and individual Rice Miller Agreement. c. Without prejudice to the joint and several liability undertaken under this Cluster Agreement, the Corporation shall be entitled to recove r the admissible dues, cost of defaulted CMR, applicable penalty and other losses from the e -BG, milling charges, amounts payable or other securities/benefits of the defaulting Rice Mill. d.

items.text: If the amount recoverable from the defaulting Rice Mill is insuffic ient to fully discharge the liability, the unrecovered balance shall constitute the joint liability of the Cluster, and the Corporation shall be entitled to recover the same from the other Cluster Members, their admissible dues, milling charges, securities/e-BGs, to the extent permissible under the applicable Government Orders, prescribed e-BG conditions and law. e. Such recovery shall be without prejudice to any other contractual, civil, revenue recovery, criminal or other action permissible under the applicable Government Orders and law. 5. Responsibility for safeguarding the Paddy received from Paddy Procurement Centres: a. The Cluster Members accept responsibility for proper accounting and safeguarding of paddy entrusted for Custom Milling until delivery and acceptance of the corresponding CMR by APSCSCL/FCI. b. Paddy and CMR shall be stored only at the authorized premises of the respective Rice Mill and shall always be maintained in a properly identifiable and countable condition for physical verification. c. The Cluster Members shall extend full cooperation to the District Administration, APSCSCL, FCI and other authorized inspection teams for physical verification of paddy, CMR, registers, electricity consumption and other relevant records. 6. Source and Authenticity of CMR: a. CMR delivered against paddy shall be produced only from the paddy received from the Paddy Procurement Centres, to the concerned designated Rice Mill. b. CMR shall not be substituted, wholly or partly, with purchased old rice, PDS rice or rice obtained from any unauthorized source. c.

The Cluster Members undertake that paddy received from PPCs shall not be sold, diverted, exchanged, transferred or otherwise disposed of except in accordance with the written instructions of the competent authority. d. Each Cluster Member shall deliver CMR strictly conforming to the quality specifications pr escribed by the Government of India / Government of Andhra Pradesh and instructions issued from time to time. b. The Rice Mills shall not deliver “Not Freshly Milled Rice”, nor mix such rice with freshly milled rice, and shall comply with the Rice Age Test / Mixed Indicator Method and other prescribed quality requirements. c. All CMR shall be delivered within the timelines communicated by the Government of India / APSCSCL. 8. Mutual Monitoring and Reporting: a. Each Cluster Member shall immediately bring to the notice of the JC & EOED / DCSM, APSCSCL any material information available to it regarding:  Shortage or diversion of paddy received from PPCs;  Unauthorized sale of Paddy stocks;  Suspected recycling/substitution of PDS rice;  Prolonged or abnormal delay in CMR delivery;  Closure/non-functioning of a Cluster Rice Mill; or  Any other serious irregularity likely to affect fulfilment of CMR obligations. b.

items.text: GOVERNMENT OF ANDHRA PRADESH ABSTRACT CA,F&CS Department — De-Centralized Procurement — Policy for Kharif Marketing Season 2026-27 – Collection of e-BGs by the Andhra Pradesh State Civil Supplies Corporation Limited (APSCSCL) for and on behalf of the State Government — Orders — Issued. CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD & CIVIL SUPPLIES (CS.II) DEPARTMENT G.O.MS.No. 17 Dated: 28-10-2026 Read the following: 1. MoU entered between Government of India and Government of Andhra Pradesh under the Decentralized Procurement Scheme. 2. G.O.Ms.No.15, Consumer Affairs, Food & Civil Supplies (CS.II) Department, dated 09.10.2026. *** ORDER: Under the Decentralized Procurement (DCP) Scheme, paddy procured from farmers at Minimum Support Price is entrusted to designated Rice Mills for Custom Milling and delivery of the resultant Custom Milled Rice (CMR) to APSCSCL/FCI. The paddy so entrusted to the Rice Mills is Government property, and adequate financial and contractual safeguards are required to protect Government interest until completion of the CMR obligations. 2. In the G.O second read above, the policy and operational framework is issued for Paddy Procurement, Custom Milling operations for KMS 2026- 27 including assessment of Rice Mills, fixation of mill-wise targets, execution of Custom Milling Agreements, submission of Electronic Bank Guarantees and execution of Cluster Agreements. 3. A Cluster Agreement mechanism is also prescribed under which participating Rice Mills in a Cluster undertake reciprocal and joint responsibility for safeguarding Government paddy stocks and fulfillment of CMR obligations.

items.text: 3. A Cluster Agreement mechanism is also prescribed under which participating Rice Mills in a Cluster undertake reciprocal and joint responsibility for safeguarding Government paddy stocks and fulfillment of CMR obligations. The Cluster Agreement provides an additional contractual safeguard to the Government, apart from the individual e-Bank Guarantee furnished by each Rice Mill. 4. After careful examination of the matter and keeping in view the need to ensure adequate security of Government paddy while differentiating between owned and leased Rice Mills and between mills with and without the additional safeguard of a Cluster Agreement, Government hereby order that the following Electronic Bank Guarantee (e-BG) norms shall be followed for allotment of paddy to Rice Mills during KMS 2026-27: Rice Mill Status Paddy Value : e- BG Value Own Rice Mill with valid Cluster Agreement 1 : 1 Leased Rice Mill with valid Cluster Agreement 1 : 1.5 Own Rice Mill without Cluster Agreement 1 : 2 Leased Rice Mill without Cluster Agreement 1 : 2.5 5. Accordingly, the following procedure shall be followed: i. No paddy shall be allotted/entrusted to any Rice Mill without availability of the prescribed e-BG coverage in the Paddy Procurement Portal. ii. The required e-BG shall be calculated with reference to the value of paddy proposed to be allotted/entrusted to the concerned Rice Mill, in the ratio applicable to the respective category indicated above. iii. The e-BG shall be furnished only in electronic form and shall be integrated through the Paddy Procurement Portal before issue of paddy. iv.

The e-BG shall remain valid and enforceable until complete discharge of all obligations arising out of the paddy entrusted for KMS 2026-27, including delivery and acceptance of CMR, settlement/disposal of resultant broken rice wherever applicable, recovery of dues/penalties, if any, and release/discharge of security by the competent authority. v. The District Civil Supplies Managers shall ensure that the available e-BG is sufficient for the value of paddy held/allotted to the Rice Mill at all times. vi. The Paddy Procurement Portal shall automatically restrict the paddy allocations to mills, whose BG is insufficient. vii. Whenever the ownership/lease status of a Rice Mill changes, the applicable e-BG requirement shall be reassessed immediately and no further paddy shall be allotted until the required additional security, if any, is furnished. 6. The reduced e-BG applicable to mills participating in a Cluster Agreement shall not dilute the primary responsibility of the individual Rice Mill to which Government paddy is physically entrusted. The joint and several liability of the other Cluster Members shall be an additional safeguard and shall operate in accordance with the terms and conditions of the prescribed Cluster Agreement. 7.

The Vice Chairman & Managing Director, APSCSCL shall make necessary modifications in the Paddy Procurement Portal to ensure automatic categorization of Rice Mills based on: i. items.title: Andhra Pradesh G.O.MS-3 dated 03/01/2025: Revenue Department - Andhra Pradesh Resurvey Project - Continuation of 679 Supernumerary Deputy Tahsildar (Re-survey) posts for the period from 23-09- 2024 to 2

items.text: 1st read above, the Government issued orders for the creation of 679 supernumerary Deputy Tahsildar posts for two years to facilitate the re- survey and recording of Gramakantam lands. These posts were created by suppressing an equal number of Senior Assistant/Revenue Inspector posts, with the condition that the suppressed posts would be restored once the supernumerary posts ceased to exist. These positions were to be filled through promotions from the feeder category, following existing procedures. 2. In the G.O. 2 nd read above, the Government designated the newly created Deputy Tahsildars (Re-Survey) as Special Executive Magistrates, granting them powers under relevant sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Central Act 2 of 1974), within their respective jurisdictions. These officers were tasked with disposing of appeals related to 9(2) and 10(2) notices issued under the APS&B Act, 1923, during the re-survey operations of agricultural lands and Gramkantam/Abadi lands until the completion of the re-survey program in their respective Mandals. 3. In the references 4 th and 5 th read above the Director of Survey. Settlements, and Land Records, A.P., Vijayawada, and the Chief Commissioner of Land Administration, A.P., Mangalagiri, proposed extending the tenure of these 679 supernumerary Deputy Tahsildar (Re-Survey) posts for an additional two years, from 23.09.2024 to 22.09.2026, to complete the re-survey and implement its findings in the remaining villages under the A.P. items.text: 2. As seen from the report of the District Collector, NTR District, in 1957, a house site patta was assigned by the then Special Deputy Tahsildar in favor of Sri Appikatla Joseph for an extent of Ac.0.10 cts. in R.S.No.147/1B of Vidyadharapuram Village, upon payment of the market value of Rs.484/- and survey charges of Rs.780/-, as evidenced by Challan No.6861 dated 23.05.1957 and Challan No.4174 dated 25.04.1957. Since then, house taxes and electricity bills have been regularly paid to VMC, Vijayawada, by the original assignee, his wife or their legal heirs in the name of the applicant’s late parents. 3. The District Collector, NTR District, reported that, as per the 22A(1)(b) list of Vidyadharapuram Village, Vijayawada an extent of Ac.0.10 Cts in R.S.No.147/1B, Ac.0.10 Cts in R.S.No.147/1C1, and Ac.0.04 Cts in R.S.No.147/1C2 is recorded as "Library - VMC." However, the library actually exists on an extent of Ac.0.025 Cts in R.S.No.147/1A, which is under the control of the Communist Party. The applicant's house is located on R.S.No.147/1B, covering Ac.0.10 Cts.

items.text: The applicant's house is located on R.S.No.147/1B, covering Ac.0.10 Cts. Property tax records in the name of (P.T.O) ::2:: Sri Appikatla Joseph, the applicant's father, under Assessment No. 4002R/6 (Old Number) dated 14.07.1988, have been verified. Subsequently, the property was transferred to the applicant's mother, Smt. A. Marthamma, under Assessment No. 34819 (New Number) dated 02.01.2012. Electricity bills are also in the names of Sri Appikatla Joseph and Smt. A. Marthamma. The applicant is currently paying house tax for Door No. 5-6-30/2 and electricity bills. 4. The District Collector, NTR District has further reported that the subject land is classified as G.P.Gunta (Water body) and no changes are incorporated in RSR. But house site patta was issued in the year 1957, Further, reported that the OTS, Regularization & Freehold schemes are not implemented in this case due to non- incorporation of classification changes in the records. 5. He has further reported that, in the instant case, although no changes are reflected in the Record of Rights in Settlement Register (RSR), it is an established fact that the assignment was made, and a house site patta was issued in 1957. The Field Measurement Book (FMB) copy clearly indicates the subdivisions in the survey number, confirming that the applicant's assigned land exists in R.S.No.147/1B, covering Ac.0.10 Cts.

items.text: The Field Measurement Book (FMB) copy clearly indicates the subdivisions in the survey number, confirming that the applicant's assigned land exists in R.S.No.147/1B, covering Ac.0.10 Cts. The applicant and their family have been in continuous possession of the land for over 60 years, supported by documents such as G.O.Ms.No.1538, dated 09.07.1955, D-Form Patta, payment of market value of Rs.484/-, and survey charges of Rs.780/- vide Challan No.6861, dated 23.05.1957, and Challan No.4174, dated 25.04.1957. Their possession is further substantiated by assessment tax records, electricity bills, and other evidence. The applicants, as legal heirs (sons) of the original assignee, continue to hold the same land throughout their lifetime. 6. Furthermore, the name of the original assignee was recorded in the Town Survey Register (TSR) copy as a house site in the Vijayawada Municipal Corporation (VMC) town records as early as 1964. This TSR entry can be considered evidence of a change in classification from Gunta (Waterbody) to house site. However, the classification in the RSR still reflects "G.P. Gunta." Once the TSR came into effect, it can be reasonably presumed that the land was converted to a house site.
items.source: Andhra Pradesh G.O.MS-340 dated 15/09/2025: Revenue (lands.IV) Department - NTR District - Prohibited properties u/s. 22-A - NTR District - Vijayawada West Mandal - Vidhyadharapuram Village - R.S.No.147/1 [REV department, 2025-09-15]
items.title: Andhra Pradesh G.O.MS-340 dated 15/09/2025: Revenue (lands.IV) Department - NTR District - Prohibited properties u/s. 22-A - NTR District - Vijayawada West Mandal - Vidhyadharapuram Village - R.S.No.147/1

items.text: However, the classification in the RSR still reflects "G.P. Gunta." Once the TSR came into effect, it can be reasonably presumed that the land was converted to a house site. Nevertheless, there is a need to incorporate changes in the RSR for this extent of Ac.0.10 Cts in R.S.No.147/1B to delete the entry from the 22A(1)(b) list and prevent future complications. 7. The District Collector, NTR, has further stated that it is not justifiable to reject the applicant's request solely due to the non-incorporation of (P.T.O) ::3:: classification changes. According to the Sub-Collector/RDO's report, the house site patta was issued long ago upon payment of survey charges and market value. At that time, it was evident that the land was not a water body, and the house site patta was granted accordingly. Administrative delays in updating the classification should not cause inconvenience to the public who are in possession and enjoyment of the property. He has further stated that government orders are required to change the classification from "G.P.-Gunta" (Waterbody) to "AWD" in this case. 8. The District Collector, NTR District has now requested the Government for necessary permission to incorporate the Changes in RSR to remove the subject House site measuring an extent of Ac.0.10 R.S.No.147/1B of Vidyadharapuram Village, Vijayawada West Mandal from 22 (A)(1)(b) List.
items.source: Andhra Pradesh G.O.MS-340 dated 15/09/2025: Revenue (lands.IV) Department - NTR District - Prohibited properties u/s. 22-A - NTR District - Vijayawada West Mandal - Vidhyadharapuram Village - R.S.No.147/1 [REV department, 2025-09-15]
items.title: Andhra Pradesh G.O.MS-340 dated 15/09/2025: Revenue (lands.IV) Department - NTR District - Prohibited properties u/s. 22-A - NTR District - Vijayawada West Mandal - Vidhyadharapuram Village - R.S.No.147/1

items.text: The CCLA & SPL.CS., A.P. has also requested to take necessary action on the report of the District Collector, NTR District. 9. The Water Resources Department have conveyed its “No Objection” to incorporate the Changes in RSR to remove the subject House site, measuring an extent of Ac.0.10 R.S.No.147/1B of Vidyadharapuram Village, Vijayawada West Mandal from the 22 (A)(1)(b) List. 10. Government after careful examination of the matter, in consultation with the Water Resources Department, hereby accord permission to the District Collector, NTR District to remove subject House site measuring an extent of Ac.0.10 R.S.No.147/1B of Vidyadharapuram Village, Vijayawada West Mandal from 22 (A)(1)(b) of Registration Act, 1908, duly changing of classification of House site measuring an extent of Ac.0.10 Cts., in R.S.No.147/1B of Vidyadharapuram Village, Vijayawada West Mandal from "G.P.-Gunta" to "AWD" 11. The Chief Commissioner of Land Administration & Special Chief Secretary, A.P. Mangalagiri, Guntur District and the District Collector, NTR District shall take further necessary action, accordingly in the matter. G. Continuously Operating Reference Station (CORS) network with the National CORS platform -Approval of Memorandum of Understanding to be entered between Government of Andhra Pradesh and Survey of India, Ministry of Science Technology, GoI – Authorization to t he Director of Survey Settlements & Land Records, A.P., Mangalagiri to sign the MoU, on behalf of Government of Andhra Pradesh - Orders - Issued. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ REVENUE (LANDS.IV) DEPARTMENT G.O.Ms.No.369 Dated:09.10.2025 ORDER: Survey of India (SoI), Department of Science and Technology, GOI, serves as the apex national mapping agency responsible for establishing and maintaining the National Spatial/Geodetic Reference Fram e (NGRF). Traditionally, this was accomplished using Ground Control Points (GCPs) and benchmarks.

items.text: Traditionally, this was accomplished using Ground Control Points (GCPs) and benchmarks. To modernize this infrastructure and meet the growing demand for high -precision, real-time positioning services, Survey of India has implemented a nationwide Continuously Operating Reference Station (CORS) network, delivering centimetre -level positional accuracy to support critical applications in land governance, logistics, infrastructure, disaster management, and research. 2. Government of Andhra Pradesh (GoA P), through its Survey, Settlements, and Land Records (SSLR) Department, established 70 state -owned Continuously Operating Reference Stations (CORS) in 2018 under the AP Resurvey Project for conducting survey of Agricultural lands, properties in habitations/ ULBs. 3. The Survey of India (SoI), the national mapping agency, manages a larger network of over 1,000 CORS stations across India to create a unified National Geodetic Reference Network. 4. The Survey of India (SoI), have proposed integrating Andhra Pradesh’s CORS network into national framework to improve efficiency, avoid duplication, and support national initiatives like Digital India. This integration requires a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), to outline how data and responsibilities will be shared. 5. The need for this integration stems from the desire to create a seamless, standardized geospatial system across India. This would enhance applications in areas like urban planning, agriculture, and scientific studies (e.g., climate change and earthquake monitoring). SoI has assured Andhra Pradesh that it will take over maintenance costs for the 70 CORS stations after the current contract expires, provide technical upgrades, and ensure the state retains ownership and recognition for its infrastructure.
